sections.title: Lesson 2.1: Characteristics of Common Stock
sections.overview: Common stock represents an ownership (equity) interest in a corporation, entitling holders to vote on major issues, share in profits through dividends, and benefit from capital appreciation. Shareholders enjoy limited liability but stand last in the liquidation hierarchy. The unit also covers the four classes of stock (authorized, issued, outstanding, treasury), market-cap categories, the dividend process, and the penny stock rules.
key_concepts: Equity = ownership; each share = proportional ownership of the corporation.
Authorized stock: maximum shares the corporate charter permits the company to issue; amendable only by stockholder vote.
Issued stock: authorized shares actually sold to investors.
Outstanding stock: issued shares currently held by the public (Issued − Treasury = Outstanding).
Treasury stock: reacquired by the issuer; carries no voting rights and pays no dividends.
Market capitalization = Outstanding shares × Current Market Value (CMV). Categories: large-cap (often 'blue chip' if mature dividend payers), mid-cap, small-cap.
Penny stock: unlisted equity trading under $5/share; classified as highly speculative.
Dividend forms: cash (default, quarterly), stock (non-taxable at receipt; cost basis adjusts), or product (rare).
Cash dividends are taxed in the year paid: nonqualified (ordinary income rates) or qualified (lower IRS-specified rate).
Four dividend dates in order: Declaration → Ex-dividend → Record → Payable.
Declaration, record, and payable dates are set by the BOD; the ex-date is set by FINRA or the listing exchange.
Ex-dividend date under T+1 settlement: same day as the record date (buy before the ex-date to receive the dividend).
Benefits of common stock: voting rights, capital appreciation, dividend income, limited liability, preemptive rights, freely transferable shares, right to inspect books and receive Form 10-K.
Voting methods: Statutory (one vote per share per seat — favors large holders); Cumulative (total votes = shares × seats, allocated freely — favors small holders).
Risks: market/value risk (price decline), dividend reduction or elimination, last priority in liquidation (residual claim).
rules: SEC Rule 3a11-1 (Securities Exchange Act of 1934): defines 'equity security.'

SEC Penny Stock Rules: Before initial solicited penny stock transaction, BD must deliver a risk disclosure document and obtain signed/dated acknowledgment; must determine suitability and obtain a signed suitability statement; must disclose the name of the stock, number of shares, current quotation, and commissions to firm and rep.
Penny stock monthly statements: required for any account holding penny stocks, regardless of activity, showing market value, share count, and issuer for each penny stock held.

Established customer exemption (penny stocks): customer with account ≥1 year (with a deposit) OR ≥3 penny stock purchases of different issuers on different days — exempt from suitability statement but NOT from disclosure.
Unsolicited penny stock transactions are exempt from suitability and disclosure rules.
Settlement: U.S.-listed equity trades settle T+1 (SEC Rule 15c6-1, as amended).
formulas: Outstanding Shares = Issued Shares − Treasury Shares
Market Capitalization = Outstanding Shares × Current Market Value per share
Stockholder's Votes (Cumulative) = Shares Owned × Number of Board Seats up for election
Stockholder's Votes per Seat (Statutory) = Shares Owned (max per seat)
mnemonics: DERP — order of dividend dates: Declaration, Ex-date, Record, Payable.
BOD sets D-R-P; Regulator (FINRA/exchange) sets E.
'Cumulative helps the small guy' — cumulative voting favors small shareholders.

sections.title: Lesson 2.2: Preferred Stock, ADRs, and Other Equity Considerations
sections.overview: Preferred stock is an equity security with bond-like fixed-income characteristics: a stated dividend (% of par; assume $100 par unless told otherwise), priority over common in dividends and liquidation, but generally no voting or preemptive rights. ADRs allow U.S. investors to hold foreign equities in dollar-denominated form. Rule 144 governs the resale of restricted and control (affiliate) stock.
key_concepts: Preferred stock: equity ownership with a fixed dividend rate; assume par = $100 unless stated.
Dividend computation: % rate × $100 par = annual dividend (paid quarterly).
Preferred shareholders generally have NO voting rights and NO preemptive rights.
Benefits: dividend preference over common; priority over common at dissolution.
Risks: purchasing power (inflation) risk, interest rate sensitivity (prices fall when rates rise), dividend may be reduced/eliminated, paid behind all creditors at dissolution.
Straight (noncumulative): missed dividends are gone forever.
Cumulative: unpaid dividends accrue as 'dividends in arrears' and must be paid in full before any common dividend.
Callable: issuer can redeem at a stated price after a stated date; often called when rates fall; dividend stops at the call date; usually includes a call premium.
Convertible: exchangeable for a fixed number of common shares; carries lower stated dividend due to upside; price tracks common once the common rises above the conversion parity.
Adjustable (variable) rate: dividend resets to a benchmark (e.g., T-bills); price is relatively stable — NOT ideal for investors seeking a FIXED income.
Participating: in addition to stated dividend, receives extra dividends up to a stated cap when profits permit.
ADR (American Depositary Receipt): negotiable U.S. security representing shares of a foreign company on deposit at a U.S. bank's foreign branch; issued and dividends paid in U.S. dollars.
ADRs trade and settle T+1 (per current SEC Rule 15c6-1 — updated from prior T+2).
ADR holder rights: may request the depositary bank cancel the ADR and deliver the underlying foreign shares; voting rights are NOT automatically passed through.
ADR risks: currency risk (dividends converted from foreign currency), political risk, market risk of underlying.
ADR dividends may be subject to foreign withholding tax; often creditable against U.S. tax liability. Capital gains taxed only in the U.S.
Rule 144 (Securities Act of 1933): governs sales of restricted securities and control (affiliate) securities.
Restricted stock: acquired in unregistered transaction (e.g., private placement); 6-month holding period (fully paid) required before resale; certificates carry a restrictive legend.
Control stock (affiliate): held by directors, officers, or 10%+ owners; family holdings aggregate.
After holding restrictions: nonaffiliates selling restricted stock have NO volume limit after 6 months; affiliates ALWAYS subject to volume limits regardless of holding period.
Form 144 filing required when an affiliate sells; allows sales over a 90-day window.
rules: Rule 144 volume limit (every 90 days): greater of 1% of outstanding shares OR average weekly trading volume over the most recent 4 weeks.
Rule 144 holding period for restricted stock: 6 months (fully paid).
Form 144 must be filed at the time of placing an order to sell by an affiliate.
formulas: Annual Preferred Dividend = Stated Rate × Par Value (assume $100 par unless told otherwise)
Quarterly Preferred Dividend = Annual Preferred Dividend ÷ 4
Rule 144 Maximum Shares Sellable (90 days) = greater of (0.01 × Outstanding Shares) OR (Average Weekly Volume over prior 4 weeks)
Average Weekly Volume = Sum of last 4 weeks' volume ÷ 4
mnemonics: Preferred = 'Bond-like equity' — fixed income, no vote, no preemptive right.
Cumulative = 'Catches up' — arrears must be paid first.
Affiliates ALWAYS limited; nonaffiliates LIMITED only during the 6-month restricted holding window.
Greater of 1% or 4-week average — the '1%-or-Average' rule.

sections.title: Lesson 2.3: Corporate Actions (Rights, Warrants, Splits, Dividends, M&A, Buybacks, Proxies)
sections.overview: Corporate actions are issuer-initiated events that affect outstanding securities — including issuing rights or warrants, paying stock dividends, splitting shares, merging, acquiring, spinning off, or buying back stock. Candidates must recognize whether each action is taxable, how it alters share count and cost basis, and the SEC notification and proxy procedures.
key_concepts: Stock (Preemptive) Rights: short-term (typically 30–45 day subscription); given to existing common shareholders; one right per share owned; subscription price is BELOW current market price; rights are tradable.
Three options for a rights holder: exercise, sell in the secondary market, or let expire.
Warrants: LONG-term (often years); usually issued as 'sweeteners' attached to bonds or preferred stock; exercise price is ABOVE the current market price at issuance.
Stock dividend: shareholder receives more shares; total position value unchanged; cost basis per share DECREASES; not taxable when received.
Forward stock split: more shares at a lower price; cost basis per share decreases; not taxable.
Reverse stock split: fewer shares at a higher price; cost basis per share increases; not taxable; often used to maintain exchange listing minimum price.
Merger: two companies combine; old shares canceled and replaced with shares of the new combined company.
Acquisition: acquirer absorbs target; target shareholders typically receive acquirer shares.
Spin-off: parent creates a new subsidiary and distributes its shares to existing parent shareholders; parent shares retained.
Buyback: issuer repurchases its own shares in the secondary market; reduces supply, can boost EPS and share price; alternative to dividends.
Tender offer: direct offer to buy securities from current owners (not through the open market); typically all-cash; used to retire debt, acquire targets, or buy convertibles.
Tax treatment summary — receive STOCK = generally non-taxable; receive CASH = generally taxable (capital gain/loss).
Stock splits and stock dividends are NEVER taxable events at the time of distribution.
Buybacks and tender offers (cash) ARE taxable — treated as a sale.
Mergers, acquisitions, and spin-offs are typically non-taxable when shares are received, but any cash portion of the consideration is taxable.

Notification: issuer must provide notice no later than 10 days before the record date (or by the record date, and never later than the effective date, in cases like rights offerings where 10 days is impractical).
Notice content: title of security, declaration date, record date, payment/distribution date, amount (cash dividend) or rate (stock dividend, split).
Proxy: limited power of attorney granting another party the right to vote a shareholder's shares; auto-revoked if shareholder attends meeting or executes a later proxy.
Street name shares: BD acts as forwarding agent for proxies and corporate communications to beneficial owners.
If a customer returns a signed proxy but does NOT indicate how to vote: the member must vote as RECOMMENDED BY MANAGEMENT.
If proxy is NOT returned by the 10th day before the meeting AND matters are MINOR: member may vote as it sees fit.
If proxy is NOT returned AND matters are MAJOR (e.g., merger, additional issuance): member may NEVER vote — shares go unvoted.
rules: SEC Rule 10b-18 (Exchange Act): safe harbor for issuer repurchases of its own equity securities (buybacks).
SEC notification of corporate actions: required disclosures to shareholders, generally at least 10 days before the record date.
Settlement for equities affected by corporate actions: T+1 (per current SEC Rule 15c6-1).
formulas: Stock Dividend — New Cost Basis per Share = Original Total Cost ÷ New Total Shares
Forward Split (a-for-b) — New Shares = Old Shares × (a ÷ b); New Price = Old Price × (b ÷ a)
Reverse Split (a-for-b, where a<b) — New Shares = Old Shares × (a ÷ b); New Price = Old Price × (b ÷ a)
Total Position Value Before Split = Total Position Value After Split (always)
Rights — Shares Purchasable = Rights Held ÷ Rights Required per New Share
mnemonics: Rights = Right Now (short term, below market); Warrants = Wait (long term, above market).
Stock for stock = no tax; cash = tax.
Splits/stock dividends: 'Same pie, more slices' — value unchanged, basis per share adjusted.
Unsigned proxy + major issue = NO VOTE. Signed-but-blank proxy = vote with MANAGEMENT.
